title: 9041 Lab Assignment 6
text:
Lab Set-Up


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(psych)      
library(ordinal)   
library(readxl)     
library(ggeffects)
library(broom)    
library(gt)    



Load and inspect the data


# A tibble: 6 × 29

6 61623     6     6     5     6     5     6     6     6     1     3     2     1
# ℹ 16 more variables: E3 <int>, E4 <int>, E5 <int>, N1 <int>, N2 <int>,
#   N3 <int>, N4 <int>, N5 <int>, O1 <int>, O2 <int>, O3 <int>, O4 <int>,
#   O5 <int>, gender <dbl>, education <chr>, age <dbl>




Question and Predictions
The bfi data contain 25 personality items from 2,800 people, five items per Big Five trait. Each item is answered on a 6-point scale from Very inaccurate to Very accurate.
The chosen trait is Extraversion. The ordered outcome is one Extraversion item, E4, “Make friends easily.” The predictor is a person’s Openness subscale score, the mean of O1 to O5 with O2 and O5 reverse-keyed. The non-centred mean of the Openness subscale is NA
If a person is more open, they will most likely be able to talk with a variety of people about a wide array of topics which will translate into making friends easily. Therefore, I predict that when people are more open, they will be more likely to make friends easily.


Data preparation


Code
# Labels for the six response options, from lowest to highest
n_levels <- c("Very inaccurate", "Moderately inaccurate", "Slightly inaccurate",
              "Slightly accurate", "Moderately accurate", "Very accurate")

# Scoring keys with reverse-keyed items
keys <- list(
  Agreeableness     = c("-A1", "A2", "A3", "A4", "A5"),
  Conscientiousness = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "-C4", "-C5"),
  Extraversion      = c("-E1", "-E2", "E3", "E4", "E5"),
  Neuroticism       = c("N1", "N2", "N3", "N4", "N5"),
  Openness          = c("O1", "-O2", "O3", "O4", "-O5")
)

scores<-scoreItems(keys, data, totals = F, min=1, max=6)

scores_df<- scores$scores

# Mutate data to include the ordered outcome, an unordered outcome, and the predictor (raw and centred)
data <- data |>
  select(E4) |>
  bind_cols(as_tibble(scores_df)) |>
  mutate(
    E4 = factor(E4, levels = 1:6, labels = n_levels, ordered = TRUE),   # The ordered outcome
    highest = factor(names(keys)[max.col(scores_df, ties.method = "first")]),  # Unordered outcome:highest-scoring trait
    open = Openness
  ) |>
  drop_na(E4, open, highest) |>
  mutate(open_c = open - mean(open))  # Centre AFTER dropping missing cases

open_bar <- mean(data$open)





Examining the Outcomes

The ordered outcome


Code
# Count how many people chose each response option for E4.
e4_counts <- data |>
  count(E4) |>
  # p is the proportion of the sample in each category, P(Y = j).
  mutate(p = n / sum(n))

Code
#plot the counts
plot_e4 <- ggplot(e4_counts, aes(x = E4, y = n, fill = E4)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = scales::label_wrap(12)) +

       x = NULL, y = "People") +

plot_e4











Showing How the Predictor Relates to the Outcome


Code
plot_jitter<-ggplot(data, aes(open, as.numeric(E4), colour = E4)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.15, alpha = 0.25, size = 1.4) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:6, labels = n_levels) +
  labs(title = "Higher Openness,\nHigher Ability to make Friends,\nwith lots of Overlap",
       x = "Openness (subscale mean, 1-6)", y = "I make friends easily") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

plot_jitter









The jitter plot shows a positive association between Openness and the tendency to endorse the item I make friends easily as higher Openness scores appear to have larger clusters along the item. However there is a lot of overlap along Openness scores and each level of agreement with the item. This makes sense as the outcome is ordinal, so although the response categories have a meaningful order, the distances between response options cannot be assumed equal. Therefore, an appropriate model should estimate the probability of an individual responding in each category rather than predicting a single numerical value especially since a predicted numeric value does not correspond to an actual response category.


The Unordered Outcome


Code
ordered_dat <- data |>
  count(highest) |>
  mutate(highest = fct_reorder(highest, n))

#plot the unordered outcome
unordered_plot <- ggplot(ordered_dat, aes(highest, n)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65, fill = "lightseagreen") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Dominant trait: five categories with no order",
       x = NULL, y = "People") +
  theme_minimal()

unordered_plot









Since each person’s dominant trait (their highest of the five subscale scores) is a set of categories with no built-in order and therefore highest is an unordered variable. For example, scoring highest on Openness is not “more” than scoring highest on Agreeableness, or vice versa.



Cumulative Probabilities

Cumulative Proportion Table


Code
#creating the table
obs_tab <- data |>
  count(E4) |>
  mutate(
    Probability = n / sum(n),
    CumulativeProbability = cumsum(Probability),
    CumulativeOdds = if_else(CumulativeProbability < 1,
                             CumulativeProbability / (1 - CumulativeProbability), NA_real_),
    Cumulative_Logodds = if_else(CumulativeProbability < 1,
                                 qlogis(CumulativeProbability), NA_real_)  
  )

# creating a clean table with gt
obs_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    E4 = "Category in E4 (j)",
    n = "n",
    Probability = "P(Y = j)",
    CumulativeProbability = "P(Y ≤ j)",
    CumulativeOdds = "Odds of ≤ j",
    Cumulative_Logodds = "Log-odds of ≤ j"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Probability, CumulativeProbability), decimals = 3) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(CumulativeOdds, Cumulative_Logodds), decimals = 3) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")

Please note that since a cumulative probability is the probability of responding with a specific response category (j) or lower, each category’s probability will increase as the probability of that response is added to the probabilities of each lower response (i.e., selecting slightly inaccurate OR moderately inaccurate OR very inaccurate). Therefore, with six categories there are five cumulative probabilities to model as the cumulative probability of the sixth category (very accurate) is 100%. This is also why the odds for any last category in cumulative probabilities has undefined odds; all categories are included in the final category so there is not a binary outcome for an odds formula to calculate the probability of not choosing any option.



Specifying and Estimating Cumulative logit Models
As I stated above, the outcome E4 - makes friends easily is ordinal - the response categories have a meaningful order (Very inaccurate < Moderately inaccurate < Slightly inaccurate < Slightly accurate < Moderately accurate < Very accurate) but the distances between response options cannot be assumed equal as people may interpret the response categories differently. Therefore, an appropriate model should estimate the probability of an individual responding in each ordered category which is why an ordinal model suits this response outcome.

Estimating the Two Nested Models


Code
# Null model: thresholds only, no predictors
null <- clm(E4 ~ 1, data = data)

# One-predictor model
one_pred <- clm(E4 ~ open_c, data = data)

summary(one_pred)

Slightly accurate|Moderately accurate     -0.39965    0.03867  -10.34

I centred Openness earlier, so that the thresholds describe a person of average Openness (4.593), rather than an impossible person scoring 0 on a 1-6 scale. Centring changes the thresholds but not the slope since the change in values will remain the same.
When reading the summary() output above, the thresholds are the points at which a response moved from one category to the next. Coefficients are the slopes which represent the effect of Agreeableness on the latent logit scale.
The estimated slope is beta = 0.12, so Higher Openness lowers the log-odds of being at or below each threshold, which shifts responses toward the higher (“accurate”) categories.


What the centred thresholds mean


Code
# plogis() turns a log-odds into a probability. 

tibble(
  Category = n_levels,
  theta = c(th, NA),
  cum = c(plogis(th), 1),
  cat_p = diff(c(0, plogis(th), 1))
) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    theta = "Threshold above category",
    cum = "P(Y ≤ j)",
    cat_p = "P(Y = j)"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(columns = theta, decimals = 2) |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(cum, cat_p), decimals = 2) |>
  sub_missing(missing_text = "—")

Applying plogis() to each threshold gives a cumulative probability and then it takes differences. For a person of average Openness, the most likely response is Moderately accurate (0.339). Their probability of endorsing the item at all, that is, Moderately accurate or lower, is the probability of Moderately accurate at 74 %.


Checking the Null Model


Code
#|label: check null

# View thresholds produced, and how they are the same as the cumulative log-odds
coef(null)


    Very inaccurate|Moderately inaccurate 
                               -2.9410498 
Moderately inaccurate|Slightly inaccurate 
                               -1.7821781 
    Slightly inaccurate|Slightly accurate 
                               -1.1464822 
    Slightly accurate|Moderately accurate 
                               -0.3956216 
        Moderately accurate|Very accurate 
                                1.0453355 


Code
obs_tab$Cumulative_Logodds[1:5]


[1] -2.9410498 -1.7821781 -1.1464822 -0.3956216  1.0453355


As can be seen with the above output, the null model has the same thresholds as the observed cumulative log-odds. This is because in a null model without any predictors, the thresholds are estimated using the cumulative log-odds from the data. The one-pred model uses Openness as a predictor, so the thresholds are now estimated using the differences in Openness. Therefore, since the predictor is included in the model, the probability of selecting different response categories is reliant on the predictor.



Comparing the Models


Code
#|label: comparing the models

# anova() on two clm models gives an LRT
lrt <- anova(null, one_pred)
lrt


Likelihood ratio tests of cumulative link models:
 
         formula:    link: threshold:
null     E4 ~ 1      logit flexible  
one_pred E4 ~ open_c logit flexible  

         no.par    AIC  logLik LR.stat df Pr(>Chisq)   
null          5 8995.5 -4492.8                         
one_pred      6 8989.8 -4488.9  7.7777  1   0.005289 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Adding Openness improves fit by a statistically significant amount, χ²(1) = 7.78, p = 0.005. The change in the degree of freedom is because the Openness model estimates one additional parameter, the Openness predictor and the χ² value and p-value shows us that including Openness signficiantly improved the fit of the model.


Code
# logLik() and AIC() pull the fit statistics from each model.
# length(coef(...)) counts the estimated parameters.
tibble(
  Model = c("Null", "Openness"),
  Parameters = c(length(coef(null)), length(coef(one_pred))),
  logLik = c(logLik(null), logLik(one_pred)),
  AIC = c(AIC(null), AIC(one_pred))
) |>
  mutate(`ΔAIC` = AIC - min(AIC)) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(logLik, AIC, `ΔAIC`), decimals = 1)

AIC agrees with the likelihood ratio test: the Openness model is preferred by a small margin (ΔAIC = 5.8).Therefore, I am choosing the Openness model (one_pred) as it improved model fit significantly (χ²(1) = 7.78, p = 0.005).

Interpretting the Slope on the Latent Scale


Code
lr_stat <- lrt$LR.stat[2]
lr_df <- lrt$df[2]
lr_p <- lrt$`Pr(>Chisq)`[2]
d_aic <- AIC(null) - AIC(one_pred)


The slope, beta = 0.1197721, is on the latent logit scale. A one-point increase in Openness moves a person’s latent “extraversion proneness” as reflected by E4 up by 0.1197721. The middle categories are each about 0.6942459 units wide on that scale, so one point of Openness shifts someone by roughly 17.2521133% of a category.



Check the Proportional Odds Assumption

Testing Proportional Odds


Code
nt <- nominal_test(one_pred)
nt


Tests of nominal effects

formula: E4 ~ open_c
       Df  logLik    AIC    LRT  Pr(>Chi)    
<none>    -4488.9 8989.8                     
open_c  4 -4478.8 8977.7 20.073 0.0004831 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The nominal test was significant (χ²(4) = 20.07, p < .001). and so I will also use a partial proportional-odds model as seen below.


Fitting a Partial Proportional Odds Model


Code
#partial odds model
m_nom <- clm(E4 ~ 1, nominal = ~ open_c, data = data)

#compare the two models to see which has superior fit

anova(one_pred, m_nom)

Interpreting the Results

Interpreting the Odds Ratio


Code

   filter(coef.type == "location")

Openness: e^beta = 1.1272399, 95% CI [1.0363083, 1.2261504], p 0.0052536. Each one-point increase in Openness multiplies the odds of responding above any threshold (for example, “Slightly accurate or higher” versus lower) by 1.1272399. That is a -13% decrease in those odds.
An odds ratio is not a change in the number of categories, and it is not a ratio of probabilities. The table below translates it into probabilities. It uses the threshold between Slightly inaccurate and Slightly accurate, so it shows the probability of endorsing the item at all:


Code
# We use the threshold between "Slightly inaccurate" and "Slightly accurate", because the model used centred Openness, I'll subtract open_bar from each raw score first.

# The model gives log-odds of being AT OR BELOW the threshold:
#     log-odds = threshold - slope * open_c

# Openness = 3
logodds_3 <- nom_est[3] - b * (3 - open_bar)   # log-odds of at or below
prob_3    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_3)         # plogis() -> probability; 1 - it = P(above)
odds_3    <- prob_3 / (1 - prob_3)         # odds of being above

# Openness = 4
logodds_4 <- nom_est[3] - b * (4 - open_bar)
prob_4    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_4)
odds_4    <- prob_4 / (1 - prob_4)

# Openness = 5
logodds_5 <- nom_est[3] - b * (5 - open_bar)
prob_5    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_5)
odds_5    <- prob_5 / (1 - prob_5)

# Openness = 6
logodds_6 <- nom_est[3] - b * (6 - open_bar)
prob_6    <- 1 - plogis(logodds_6)
odds_6    <- prob_6 / (1 - prob_6)

prob_tab <- tibble(
  Openness = c(3, 4, 5, 6),
  Prob = c(prob_3, prob_4, prob_5, prob_6),
  Odds = c(odds_3, odds_4, odds_5, odds_6)
)

prob_tab |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(Prob = "P(Slightly accurate or higher)") |>
  fmt_number(columns = c(Prob, Odds), decimals = 2)

Each one-point step multiplies the odds by 1.1272399, which is the OR. The probability, however, falls by -0.0298884 from 3 to 4 and -0.0297402 from 5 to 6. A constant odds ratio implies different probability changes depending on where you start, which is why we also plot predicted probabilities.


Plotting Predicted Category Probabilities


Code
# ggpredict() returns one row per Openness value x response category.
pred <- ggpredict(m_nom, terms = "open_c [all]")




Code
pred |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(
    response.level = factor(response.level,
                            labels = n_levels),
    open = x + open_bar   
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(open, predicted, fill = response.level)) +
  geom_area(position = "stack") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(title = "Predicted probability of each response to E4:\n'Make friends easily'",
       x = "Openness (subscale mean)", 
       y = "Predicted probability", fill = NULL) 









At all levels of Openness the probability mostly sits in the “accurate” categories but at low Openness, more of the probability sits in the “inaccurate” categories than at high Openness. As Openness rises, it moves more toward Moderately accurate and Very accurate. At every value of Openness, the six probabilities sum to 1, which is why the stack always reaches 100%.


Coefficient Plot of Cumulative Odds Ratios


Code
bind_rows(
  tibble(Threshold = "Shared (proportional odds)", OR = or_tab$estimate,
         low = or_tab$conf.low, high = or_tab$conf.high, type = "Shared"),
  threshold_or |> transmute(Threshold, OR, low, high, type = "Threshold-specific")
) |>
  mutate(Threshold = fct_rev(fct_inorder(Threshold))) |>   # keep thresholds in order, top to bottom
  ggplot(aes(OR, Threshold, colour = type)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +  # OR = 1 means no effect
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = low, xmax = high)) +
  labs(title = "Cumulative odds ratios per point of Openness",
       x = "Odds ratio (responding above the threshold)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")









None of the intervals sit well below 1 (the dashed line), and two intervals sit well above 1. The threshold-specific estimates also vary in size across the response categories, rather than consistently matching the shared odds ratio from the proportional-odds model. This suggests that the effect of Openness differs depending on the threshold which provides further evidence that the proportional-odds assumption was violated and the partial proportional-odds model was more appropriate.



8. Results paragraph
I fit a cumulative logit (proportional-odds) model predicting responses to “Make friends easily” from mean-centred Openness (N= 2,791). Openness improved fit over a null model, χ²^2(1) = 7.78, p rround(lr_p, 3)`. As predicted, more open people were more likely to endorse the item, OR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.04, 1]: each one-point increase in Openness increased the odds of a higher response by about 12.7%. However. the proportional-odds assumption did not hold, χ²(4) = 20.07, p 0. Therefore, a partial proportional-odds model was estimated, allowing the effect of Openness to vary across the five response thresholds.
The threshold-specific odds ratios showed that the association between Openness and response endorsement varied across the response scale (Figure: Cumulative odds ratios per point of Openness). At the two lowest thresholds, the odds ratios were 0.91 (95% CI [0.75, 1.11]) and 0.9 (95% CI [0.79, 1.02]), respectively, with both confidence intervals including 1. The association became stronger at the higher thresholds, with odds ratios of 1.15 (95% CI [1.04, 1.27]) and 1.23 (95% CI [1.1, 1.38]). Both of these confidence intervals were above 1. This suggests that Openness was more strongly associated with endorsing the higher response categories, supporting the use of the partial proportional-odds model.
